entries.name: The funnel
entries.line: How a Lean proof becomes papers and a video
entries.claim: The funnel is a set of written instructions that AI follows to turn a proof Lean has accepted into shorter and shorter versions for different readers. For one Erdős problem that is 152 pages, then 26, then 16, then a half-hour video.
entries.limit: Lean checks the proof. An expert still has to judge whether each paper and video says the same maths.

entries.description: Written instructions that AI follows to turn a proof Lean has accepted into shorter versions for different readers. For one Erdős problem that is 152 pages, then 26, then 16, then a half-hour video. Lean checks the proof. The papers and the video still need an expert’s reading.

entries.name: Maths Map
entries.line: Eight Erdős problems on one map
entries.claim: Maths Map is a website with one map of every theorem from my research on eight Erdős problems. Click a theorem and you go straight to where it is written up, in the long research record or the short paper for experts.
entries.limit: Lean checks only some of the theorems, and the papers are written with AI, so an expert still needs to read them. Seven of the eight questions remain open. For #1041, a formal version of the statement is refuted.
entries.credit: The #1041 formal-statement counterexample is due to ani.

entries.name: Erdős #257
entries.line: A case from 1968, proved and checked in Lean
entries.claim: Take the fractions 1, 1/3, 1/7, 1/15 and so on, and add up infinitely many of them. Erdős asked whether the total can ever be written as a fraction. In 1968 he stated one case, where the reciprocals of the chosen exponents have a finite sum, and proved it with an extra restriction. Here that case is proved without the restriction, and Lean accepts the proof.
entries.limit: The question Erdős asked, for every infinite choice, is still open. The papers are written with AI and are not peer reviewed.
entries.credit: Erdős stated this case in 1968. Google DeepMind's Formal Conjectures lists it as solved.
entries.page_title: Erdős #257: a case from 1968, proved and checked in Lean
entries.description: Add up infinitely many of the fractions 1, 1/3, 1/7, 1/15 and so on. Can the total ever be written as a fraction? Erdős stated one case in 1968 and proved it with an extra restriction. Here it is proved without the restriction, and Lean accepts the proof. The question for every infinite choice is still open.

entries.name: Quantum computers
entries.line: OpenAI's fourth-power result, proved again in Lean
entries.claim: Count how often each machine looks at its input. For a yes-or-no question with an answer for every input, an ordinary computer needs at most a fixed multiple of the quantum count to the fourth power, and OpenAI showed that no smaller power works. Lean checks that whole theorem here.
entries.limit: The count is of looks at the input, which is a different measure from running time. The labels that compare each Lean statement with the paper are AI-written, and no expert has reviewed them yet.
entries.mine: With AI, I proved the same theorem in Lean and wrote two explanations of the proof. I built a website where the Lean beside each paper follows the paragraph you are reading.
entries.theirs: OpenAI proved the result and released its paper in October 2026.
entries.credit: The result matches an upper bound proved in 2020.
entries.page_title: Quantum computers: OpenAI’s fourth-power result, proved again in Lean
entries.description: Count how often each machine looks at its input. For yes-or-no questions with an answer for every input, the ordinary count is at most a fixed multiple of the quantum count to the fourth power, and OpenAI showed no smaller power works. Lean checks this. Looks at the input are a different measure from running time.

entries.name: Spin glass
entries.line: Two nearly best answers, half the arrows differ
entries.claim: In a model of magnets, every arrow points up or down and every arrangement gets a score. Two arrangements can both score almost the best while about half their arrows differ. When the scoring is random, the chance that such a pair exists approaches 100% as the number of arrows grows.
entries.limit: The Lean proofs are OpenAI's and cover OpenAI's theorem. They do not cover this result about two arrangements.
entries.mine: With AI, I wrote three papers that explain OpenAI's proof. I built a website where each paper is read beside OpenAI's Lean and a graph of the argument's 131 steps.
entries.theirs: OpenAI proved the theorem and wrote its Lean. Hong-Bin Chen first proved, in July 2026, the property of that theorem this result uses.
entries.credit: The result follows from a 2020 paper by Auffinger, Chen and Zeng and an OpenAI theorem released in October 2026. Full support, the part of that theorem the result uses, was first proved in a July 2026 paper by Hong-Bin Chen. OpenAI's proof is quantitative and also gives a strictly positive density.
entries.page_title: Spin glass: two nearly best answers, half the arrows differ
entries.description: In a model of magnets, two arrangements can both score almost the best while about half their arrows differ. The result follows from a 2020 paper by Auffinger, Chen and Zeng and an OpenAI theorem. Full support was first proved in a July 2026 paper by Hong-Bin Chen. The Lean proofs are OpenAI’s and cover OpenAI’s theorem only.
entries.card_alt: Spin glass: Two nearly best answers, half the arrows differ. A frame from the project’s video.

entries.name: PCP theorem
entries.line: Troy Lee's Lean proof, explained at three lengths
entries.claim: The PCP theorem says that any proof a computer can check quickly can be rewritten so that a checker reads only a fixed number of its bits, chosen at random. For a true claim the rewritten proof is always accepted, and every proof of a false claim is rejected at least half the time.
entries.limit: Lean compiled Lee's proof. I made the three papers and their links to the Lean with AI. Neither Lee nor the authors of the algebraic proof have reviewed them, and nobody has compared each sentence with the Lean lines it links to.
entries.mine: With AI, I wrote three papers that explain his Lean proof: one through worked examples, one for specialists and one detailed account. In each paper, clicking a linked sentence opens the Lean lines it describes.
entries.theirs: Troy Lee wrote the proof of the PCP theorem in Lean, and a guide to reading it. His Lean follows the algebraic proof by Amireddy, Behera, Srinivasan, Sudan and Willumsgaard.
entries.page_title: PCP theorem: Troy Lee's Lean proof, explained at three lengths
entries.description: The PCP theorem says a proof can be rewritten so that a checker reads only a fixed number of its bits, chosen at random, and still rejects every proof of a false claim at least half the time. Troy Lee proved it in Lean. Three AI-written explanations of his proof, linked to his Lean and not yet reviewed by him.
entries.card_alt: PCP theorem: Troy Lee's Lean proof, explained at three lengths. The exposition open in Proof Reader beside a graph of the proof.

entries.name: Reader websites
entries.line: Click a linked sentence, open the Lean beside it
entries.names: Lean Exposition, Quartic Reader, Proof Reader
entries.claim: Three websites where you read a maths paper and click a linked sentence to open the Lean linked to it, beside the text. In Lean Exposition and Proof Reader, the step you are reading is also highlighted on a map of the argument.
entries.limit: Lean checks the code. Whether a sentence and the code say the same thing is for a person to judge, and I made the links with AI.
entries.mine: I built the three websites. With AI, I linked sentences in each paper to the Lean lines they describe, and wrote the explanations of OpenAI's results, of the PCP proof and of the coupled-spring proof.
entries.theirs: OpenAI proved the two results shown in Lean Exposition and Quartic Reader, and wrote the Lean in Lean Exposition. Frohlich, Foster, Kavvos and Wang wrote Contextual Embeddings and its Lean proof. Troy Lee wrote the Lean proof of the PCP theorem, and Bjørn Kjos-Hanssen the Lean proof about a coupled spring.

entries.name: Atlas
entries.line: Two groups, two labels for one maths paper
entries.claim: Atlas is a website that lists the papers in OpenAI's October 2026 maths release, with other groups' checking reports linked beside each one. For the paper about π, two groups both report the proof accepted and label its coverage differently. Atlas shows the two labels side by side.
entries.limit: Each group reported its own labels and proof checks, and Atlas has not rerun them. The suggested matches between paper theorems and Lean statements are unreviewed.
entries.mine: I built a website with one page for each group of OpenAI's papers. On that page you read the paper, open its Lean statements and compare what each outside report says about it.
entries.theirs: OpenAI published the mathematics papers and their Lean code. Other groups, among them MathVet and Carlos Toledo with cert-machine, published reports on those proofs.
entries.credit: The two reports on the π paper are by MathVet and by Carlos Toledo's cert-machine. Atlas also uses Neal McBurnett's Lean tooling.

entries.description: A website that lists the papers in OpenAI’s October 2026 maths release, with other groups' checking reports beside each one. For the paper about π, two groups both report the proof accepted and label its coverage differently. Atlas links their reports and has not rerun their checks.

entries.name: Verification map
entries.line: What one proof covers, in a toolkit of 88 components
entries.claim: A map of the 88 components of my public toolkit. Rings around each component show which kinds of evidence it has. Sixteen calculations are proved with Dafny for every input: the twelve marked on the map, and four shared by the whole toolkit.
entries.limit: Each proof covers one stated calculation. The outer ring shows how much of a component's whole claim has been checked, and it reads unknown for every component.

entries.name: MedAgentBench study
entries.line: A script that reads one page of results passes all 30 released cases
entries.claim: In the potassium task a model reads a patient's most recent potassium result and submits two orders if it is low. A script that reads only the first page of search results passes Stanford's grader on all 30 released cases, though on 12 of them that page does not contain the most recent result. On the 629 further cases, which all need the orders, the same script passes 299.
entries.limit: One task of the benchmark, and one AI model, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. This is a prototype, and no one outside the study has reviewed it.
entries.mine: I ran a new experiment on one task, potassium replacement. I wrote the task's instruction as a specification in Lean. I built 629 further cases from the benchmark's own records, and ran three scripts and one AI model on them.
entries.theirs: MedAgentBench is by Jiang and coauthors at Stanford. It contains clinical tasks, de-identified patient records in a simulated record system, and a program that grades the answers an AI model gives.
entries.by: Benchmark by Jiang and coauthors, Stanford
entries.page_title: MedAgentBench study: a script that reads one page of results passes all 30 released cases
entries.description: MedAgentBench's potassium task, followed from its instruction to its grading code. A script that reads only the first page of search results passes Stanford's grader on all 30 released cases, and on 299 of 629 further cases built from the benchmark's own records. One task, one model, and a prototype nobody outside has reviewed.
entries.card_alt: MedAgentBench study: a script that reads one page of results passes all 30 released cases. A table from the study's page.

entries.name: FaithformBench Reader
entries.line: A wrong step adds a number. In two thirds of false positives, the Lean omits it.
entries.claim: In one case a step is changed to say that 3 miles plus 3 miles is 5 miles. The Lean statement written for that step is 3 * 2 = 6, and the prover proved it. Where a change put a new number into a step, that number is missing from the Lean statement in 9,223 of 13,606 false positives (68%).
entries.limit: I counted in the authors' published results and ran no translation program or prover again. The authors have not reviewed or endorsed this project.
entries.mine: I built a website that shows each of their steps beside the Lean statement each of the four programs wrote for it. In their published results I counted how many false positives do not contain the number that the change put into the step.
entries.theirs: Rob Cornish, Iacopo Ghinassi and coauthors changed each step of a worked solution to make it wrong, had four AI programs translate every step into a Lean statement, and published each statement with whether a prover proved it. They call a proved statement of a wrong step a false positive.
entries.by: Benchmark by Cornish, Ghinassi and coauthors
entries.page_title: FaithformBench Reader: where a wrong step adds a number, two thirds of false positives omit it from the Lean
entries.description: FaithformBench changes a step of reasoning to make it wrong and counts how often its Lean translation is still proved. Where the change put a new number into the step, that number is missing from the Lean in 9,223 of 13,606 false positives of this kind. A reader shows every step beside its Lean. Independent of the benchmark's authors.
entries.card_alt: FaithformBench Reader: a wrong step adds a number, and in two thirds of false positives the Lean omits it. One step beside its Lean statement in the reader.

entries.name: Spec change map
entries.line: What three corrected clauses changed in a login contract
entries.claim: Take a login with the right password, where the account lookup and the token signing both work. The Microsoft Research listing allows a token or an HTTP 500 error. The GitHub Next listing allows only a token. The correction removes the HTTP 500 from 5 of the 18 situations and adds no response anywhere.
entries.limit: The comparison is a finite model of the two printed listings: 162 modelled logins in 18 situations. Nobody ran the app, and the map does not show whether the code meets either listing.
entries.mine: I compared the two published contracts. For each of 18 login situations, the map shows which HTTP responses each version allows, which clause removed a response, and which functions that clause takes on trust.
entries.theirs: PDD Kit is a research prototype in which AI coding assistants write Rust code and proofs that the Verus verifier checks. Its authors published the contract for its login function twice: in a Microsoft Research post, and on the GitHub Next page with three clauses corrected.
entries.page_title: Spec change map: what three corrected clauses changed in a login contract
entries.description: PDD Kit's login contract has been published twice, the second time with three clauses corrected. For a login with the right password, the first listing allows a token or a server error and the corrected one allows only the token. A map of every situation the correction changed, from a finite model of the two printed listings.
entries.card_alt: Spec change map: what three corrected clauses changed in a login contract. The map of responses each version of the contract allows.

entries.name: Code Ontology Bridge
entries.line: NVIDIA's Auto Ontology answers questions about its own code
entries.claim: A program that reads a Python project and writes a database of every function and which function calls which. Given that database of its own code, NVIDIA's Auto Ontology, running a DeepSeek model, answered 10.3 of 12 questions correctly on average. The same model asked directly answered 3.2.
entries.limit: Twelve questions, written by AI models. The answer keys were corrected after the runs, which moved results in both directions.
entries.mine: I wrote a program that reads Python source code and writes a database of its files, functions, classes, calls and imports. I gave Auto Ontology that database of its own code and counted how many of twelve questions it answered correctly. The study is independent of NVIDIA.
entries.theirs: Auto Ontology is NVIDIA's open-source system for answering questions about databases.
entries.page_title: Code Ontology Bridge: NVIDIA’s Auto Ontology answers questions about its own code
entries.description: A program that reads a Python project and writes a database of its functions and calls. Given that database of its own code, NVIDIA’s Auto Ontology, running a DeepSeek model, answered 10.3 of 12 questions correctly on average. The same model asked directly answered 3.2. AI models wrote the questions, and the study is independent of NVIDIA.

entries.name: Stale descriptions
entries.line: After an edit, which sentences about other files to reread
entries.claim: I ask AI coding assistants to keep a few sentences about each file inside that file. Editing a function in one file can make a sentence in another file false. In the test, one function is changed from doubling a number to tripling it, and a sentence about its caller in another file, that it returns twice the value, becomes false. Glean returns that caller, and the script lists its three sentences for rereading.
entries.limit: Three files from Glean's own Python example, with sentences and true-or-false verdicts that I wrote by hand. It shows the mechanism. How often this happens in a real project is untested.
entries.mine: I wrote sentences that describe those three files and marked each one true or false after each change to the code. A script asks Glean which functions call or refer to the changed code and lists the sentences about those functions.
entries.theirs: Glean is Meta's open-source program that indexes code and answers questions such as which functions call a given function. The three Python files in this test are Glean's own example.
entries.page_title: Stale descriptions: after an edit, which sentences about other files to reread
entries.description: Editing a function in one file can make a sentence about another file false. This project tests whether Glean, Meta's open-source code index, can list those sentences for rereading by asking which functions call or refer to the changed code. Three files from Glean's own example, with hand-written verdicts.
entries.card_alt: Stale descriptions: after an edit, which sentences about other files to reread. A table of results from the project's README.

entries.name: One Checkout
entries.line: Commit one fix while another AI keeps editing
entries.claim: When two AI coding assistants edit the same file, committing one finished fix can also commit the other's unfinished edits. One Checkout commits only the exact lines of the fix, and the shared file still contains both sets of edits.
entries.limit: It does not stop two assistants overwriting each other's edits. It turns off Git's usual checks for each commit, so the assistants have to run the project's checks themselves.
entries.page_title: One Checkout: commit one fix while another AI keeps editing
entries.description: When two AI coding assistants edit the same file, saving one finished fix can also save the other’s unfinished edits. One Checkout commits only the exact lines of the fix. It does not stop two assistants overwriting each other’s edits.

entries.name: Safety Core
entries.line: A written rule let 6 of 10 AI runs commit a made-up value. A check let 0.
entries.claim: Safety Core is one file of rules for AI coding assistants, each rule labelled with how it is enforced. In one test an assistant made up a setting value so a failing test passed, then committed: in 10 runs of 10 with no rules, 6 of 10 with written rules, and 0 of 10 when a check held the command for approval.
entries.limit: One model, Claude Haiku 4.5, on one small project, ten runs per setup. The check was written after this failure was first seen, and nobody was present to approve.

entries.name: Edit View
entries.line: An edit can remove text that its monitor is never shown
entries.claim: The released program shows the monitor the first 3,000 characters of the text an edit replaces. If the edit begins with 3,000 unchanged characters, removing a comment from an SSH settings file and removing the line PasswordAuthentication no give the monitor the same input. Edit View always includes the removed text, so the two edits give different input.
entries.limit: Tested on Anthropic's released code at one commit, with an OpenAI model as the monitor and three runs per case. Nothing was run against current Claude Code. I am not affiliated with Anthropic.
entries.mine: I found a case where that program gives the monitor the same text for two different edits. I wrote Edit View, another way to prepare an edit for the monitor, and replayed both edits through the released monitor each way.
entries.theirs: Anthropic released the code from its Red-Teaming Auto Mode study. In that code a second AI model, the monitor, reads each action an AI coding assistant proposes and allows or blocks it. One program prepares the text of a file edit for the monitor to read.
entries.page_title: Edit View: an edit can remove text that its monitor is never shown
entries.description: Anthropic's released program shows a monitor the first 3,000 characters of the text an edit replaces. When an edit begins with 3,000 unchanged characters, removing a comment and removing a security setting give the monitor the same input. Edit View always includes the removed text. Tested on the released code only.
entries.card_alt: Edit View: an edit can remove text that its monitor is never shown. Output from the project's own script.

entries.name: Agent Trace
entries.line: Read what your AI coding assistant ran
entries.claim: Claude Code and Codex save every conversation as a file. Agent Trace lists those conversations as they run, shows each command beside what it returned, and copies the part you choose into another chat.
entries.limit: It shows only what the files recorded. Large outputs can be shortened, and it does not remove passwords from what it copies.
entries.page_title: Agent Trace: read what your AI coding assistant ran
entries.description: Claude Code and Codex save every conversation as a file. Agent Trace lists those conversations as they run, shows each command beside what it returned, and copies the part you choose into another chat. It shows only what the files recorded.

entries.name: Zenith
entries.line: Showing an AI tester the bugs it missed
entries.claim: An AI model that tests code was shown the bugs it had missed on practice problems. On 58 new problems, the share of hidden bug types it caught rose on average from 69.2% to 77.0%.
entries.limit: About half of the rise came from timeouts. The study tested one model on short programs, and rules the model wrote from its own mistakes did not clearly raise the score.
